opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a really interesting question, and honestly it's one we didn't think about much at the beginning. When I started working on legged locomotion with reinforcement learning, the goal was pretty much: get the robot to walk, don't fall, track the velocity command. "Optimal" was defined entirely by the reward function, and the reward function only cared about the task and some regularization so the motors wouldn't overheat or the motions wouldn't be too jittery.

What you learn quickly, though, is that "optimal" according to the reward is not the same as "good." RL is very good at exploiting whatever you give it. If you don't constrain it, you get gaits that technically work but look strange: very high-frequency stepping, weird foot placements, the robot vibrating in place. In a lab that's fine. Next to a person it's unsettling, and people don't trust it.

So in practice, comfort becomes part of the objective. A lot of it is smoothness: penalizing joint accelerations and action rates, encouraging regular, predictable gaits, limiting how fast the base can accelerate. Some of it is legibility. You want the robot's motion to communicate its intent, so a person can look at it and roughly know where it's going next. Humans are very good at reading other humans' and animals' motion, and if the robot moves in a way that matches those expectations, people relax.

There's a tradeoff, but I'd argue it's smaller than people think. Smooth, natural motions are often more energy-efficient and more robust, and they transfer better from simulation to the real robot, because the simulator models those regimes more accurately than aggressive, high-frequency behavior. The real cost is mostly in peak performance, like top speed or the most aggressive recovery. For a robot working around people, you rarely need that peak. You can keep it in reserve for safety-critical moments, like catching itself when it slips, and run a calmer behavior the rest of the time.

The other piece is that comfort is context-dependent. In an empty warehouse you can let the robot move more efficiently and quickly. In a home, or near a child, you want it slower, more conservative, and more predictable. So I think the right approach isn't one fixed balance. It's policies that can be conditioned on context, where the system, or the people deploying it, can shift the balance toward caution when humans are close.

And ultimately, safety and comfort aren't something you bolt on at the end. If you want robots in human spaces, they have to be part of how you define success from the start.

r001.rationale: The response says robots near people should use calmer, slower, more predictable behavior for comfort, even at a cost to peak performance.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a tension we run into constantly, especially with legged robots. When you train a locomotion policy with reinforcement learning, the optimizer doesn't care about anything you didn't put in the reward. If you reward speed and energy efficiency, you can get gaits that are technically great but look jittery, twitchy, or just strange. The robot might vibrate its legs at high frequency because that happens to be efficient in simulation, or it might take an unusually direct path that brings it very close to a person. From the controller's point of view that's optimal. From the person's point of view it's unsettling.

So in practice, "optimal" has to include the human. I tend to think of comfort less as a constraint that fights performance and more as part of the objective that was always missing. We add terms for smoothness, for limiting joint accelerations and torque rate, for keeping the base stable, for predictable foot placements. Those aren't just aesthetics. Smooth motion also tends to be more robust and better for the hardware, so the trade-off is often smaller than people expect. You give up a few percent in some nominal metric and get motion that people can actually read and anticipate.

The harder part is the social layer: how close the robot passes, whether it slows down when approaching someone, whether its intent is legible. Humans are very good at predicting other humans and quite bad at predicting a quadruped that moves in a way nothing in nature does. So I'd rather the robot be slightly slower and very predictable than fast and surprising. If people can't guess what it's about to do, they don't trust it, and then it doesn't matter how good the controller is because nobody wants it in the building.

The honest answer is that we don't have a clean formula for this yet. A lot of it is still iterating with real people, watching their reactions, and folding that back into training. But my rule of thumb is that around people, legibility and smoothness are part of the performance spec, not something you trade away for it.

r001.rationale: The response says a robot may give up some nominal performance and move more slowly to be predictable and comfortable around people.

astra-6.text:
I think the first question is what we mean by optimal. If you optimize purely for speed or energy efficiency, you might get a motion that works very well for the robot but feels quite strange to someone standing next to it. So, for a robot operating around people, predictability and comfort have to be part of the objective as well.

That doesn’t necessarily mean the robot should move exactly like a human. It means people should be able to understand what it’s doing and anticipate where it will go. You might accept a slightly slower movement if it gives someone more space or avoids an abrupt change in direction.

The difficult part is turning that into something you can train for. We can measure energy consumption fairly directly; human comfort is much more dependent on the person and the context. So I would treat safety as a constraint, then evaluate the trade-off between task performance and comfort with people, rather than assuming that a motion that looks good to us as researchers will feel good to everyone.

r001.rationale: The response says a robot may accept slightly slower movement when that gives people more space or avoids abrupt changes, making comfort part of its movement objective.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you first have to ask what you mean by optimal. If you optimize only for speed or energy efficiency, you might get a motion that works very well for the robot but feels quite unsettling to a person standing next to it. So human comfort has to be part of the objective, together with constraints on safety.

For example, a robot might be able to move past you very quickly without making contact, but you don’t necessarily know that. Giving you more space and moving in a predictable way could be the better behavior, even if it takes a little longer. The challenge is that comfort is harder to quantify than something like energy consumption. You need to evaluate how people actually respond, rather than assuming that a motion that looks good to us as roboticists will feel comfortable to everyone.

r001.rationale: It says giving people more space and moving predictably can be better even if it takes longer, making comfort a priority over optimal speed or efficiency.
